en: The Kramakārikā Śikṣā. Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa!
Having prostrated before the Primordial Sun, the crest-jewel of the lords of yogis, [I shall compose this work].
To the omniscient Yājñavalkya and his disciple, the sage Kātyāyana,
we now commence this *kārikā* concerning the rules for the sequence and conclusion of all the mantras of the Vājasaneyaka, which belongs to the Yajurveda.
In the *śloka*, [the sandhi] devoid of *bindu* and so forth is not difficult to endure; in the *pratīkas*, however, it is unavoidable.
The nominative, genitive, and locative cases are each appropriately employed.
This sequence proceeds according to the order of the words.

Kātyāyana declared that there is no fixed order for those ending in the *gaṇa* [of consonants]. Furthermore, others have described [the types of binding] as single-winding (*ekaveṣṭi*), double-winding (*dviveṣṭi*), triple-winding (*triveṣṭi*),
four-winding (*caturveṣṭi*), middle-winding (*madhyaveṣṭi*), and five-winding (*pañcaveṣṭi*).
The general rule is that there shall be an avagraha at the end of an anuvāka, at the end of a half-verse (ardharca), likewise for ṛks,
and at the terminations of sentences of yajus-mantras. This [work], composed by Śrī Śambhumishra, is a direct exposition of Yājñavalkya.
Let the *ratnamālā* manual be composed by those with throats trained in the sequence:

for when a short vowel is followed by an *anusvāra*, it becomes possessed of a long *anusvāra*, provided there is no doubling (*dveśa*) of the following consonant; however, this is not the case during the time of the horses' [recitation] in the sequential order.
Oṃ! This chapter beginning with "iṣe tvā" is indeed wrapped at the end of its sections; it is triple-wrapped with the Gāyatrī meter, whereas previously it was triple-wrapped in a harsh manner.
With "deva savitar," the threefold [meter] is one; thus, this is your double wrapping.
These two and one constitute the *anuvāka* of Agni and Soma;

"O Agni, for the unassailable" is the single verse (*ekavṛt*), "The gods, who know the way" is the double-verse (*dvivṛt*), the group of six beginning with "sambarhya" is the single-verse, and "O wide-striding Viṣṇu" is the double-extension (*dviveṣṭana*). 10–11.
Then, for the *asiddha*, there is one [verse] consisting of three and four [feet], "saṃ vārccā" with two enclosures;
for the *yajñasañc* in the state of unity, "agnaye kavya" has no enclosure.
For "yerū," there are two enclosures; "namo" has two and one; at the beginning and end, "ūrjjarūpa" has two enclosures.
In the eight [verses] beginning with *samidh*, fire (*agni*) is doubled; light (*jyotis*) is six and one.
Indra is fivefold and should be surrounded; the fuel-stick (*samid*) has five enclosures.
Even in the six following [verses], the body (*tanūpāt*) is doubled; seven and one. 13–14.
Having taken up [the verses], there is a double wrapping at the end of the five;
for the eight beginning with "Soma-ādyam," there is a double wrapping around the outside; the "dūḍabha" verse is triple-wrapped;
the single section of the *anuvāka* beginning with "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ"; and the section beginning with "praghāsinaḥ" has a double wrapping.

The verses ending with *yad agrāmā* are for the *antaveṣṭi*; *mo ṣū ṇaḥ* is for two [verses], repeated twice. 16. Those ending with *avabhṛtha* are for the *antaveṣṭi*; for the eight [verses] beginning with *pūrṇād arviḥ*, there is a repetition of two.
This is for the *aikāhika*; for the two *tryambaka* verses, there is a repetition of two, followed by the final repetition (*antavṛt*). 17.
*vājinītvājo* has two enclosures; *vājyahampañca* has one enclosure;
*edamādi* has three; *dvivṛt* among the *mahīnām* has one enclosure; *āpo* has two enclosures; *svāhā yajñam* has an enclosure at the end. 18.
For Ākūti, for Prayuj, the Trivṛt; the Viśva of the God is the Dvivṛt (19).
Make the fourfold unity of the Ṛc and Sāman thy vow; sevenfold is the oneness.
Thou art the guardian of the vow through Agni, the Dvivṛt; the five are the encirclers within their own realm (20).
This is your fivefold-oneness; the Vasus and others are your fourfold-oneness;
this is your twofold-oneness, which is bound twice around from the beginning to the end. "For the sake of progeny, thee"—this is the binding at the end of the first half.
In the *sagma* [hymn], there is the unity of four [verses] beginning with *ardhaśukra* and *tapas*; in the *pratipanthin*, there is the doubling of the *veṣṭya*; in the *aditya*, the skin is doubled;
in the *vana*, there is the doubling of the two *yugas*; and in the *srāva*, there is the unity of the *yuga*. 22–23.
Homage to Mitra’s two-fold [hymn] and to Varuṇa’s three-fold, the highest;
the body of Agni is a union of oneness—may there be for us twofold duality. 24.
May Indra’s roar fall upon you, encompassing you with its recitations.
In the three [verses] beginning with "yuñjate," there is a combination of two, one, and one;

in the three [verses] beginning with "viṣṇoḥ" and so on, there is a combination of two, one, and one; in the verse ending with "viṣṇor arāṭam," there is a combination of five and one; and in "yavo 'si," there is a combination of four and one. 25–26.
"Pari tvā girvaṇaḥ" has two *dvṛt*s; "indrasya syūḥ" has three *rathāntara*s; "vibhūr asi" consists of a single *anuvāka*; "jyotiḥ" possesses four *veṣṭaka*s.
(27) "agne naya" has two [verses]; "deva savitar" has three [verses] and one [verse].
For this [hymn] consisting of the unity of the three exceeds the others; it has two enclosures (dviveṣṭana).
The leader (agreṇīr) is within the growth (antavṛd), while the one beyond the three is the enclosure at the end (dvivṛtparo'ntavṛt).
And the "upāvīr" [verse] is that which follows the section beginning with "aśca manaste yat te tvā. (28–29)
The unification of the four beginning with the ocean is "this water" (āpaḥ); for two [verses], there is a double winding.
For Agni, there should be windings around the base of the object; those [verses] which have two windings are used.
By "hṛde tvā," there is a unity of pairs; "śṛṇotu agniḥ" has two windings.
The verses "devīrāpaḥ," "trayaikatvam," and "yamagne pṛtsu" constitute a *dvivṛt* (31).
The verse "tvamaṅga" consists of seven *ekas* (units) and is threefold (*triveṣṭanaḥ*).
There is a triad of *vācas*, a pair of *upayāmas*, and a *dvivṛt* for the teacher (32).

O Indra and Vāyu, this [offering] is for you both; with wealth, as you two are the three-fold encompassers, may it increase from of old. Seeking the pure through the double-turning, he moves within the enclosure.
In the four [verses] of the unbroken one, this double-turning is the longing one; you are the middle.
This [cup] is for you, being extremely wrapped; those who are gods are doubly wrapped (dviveṣṭana). 34. For Agni there is oneness, for Indra there is oneness; the head is doubly wrapped.
It should be internally wrapped for the Upāṃśu; the waters and the gods are doubly wrapped. 35.
The *vṛṣṇa-ūrmi* is the unity of the three; Savitṛ is the mode of the *anuvāka*; the brilliance of Soma is the oneness with Yama; the *sadhamādī* is the double-enveloping.
(36) The *kṣatrasya ulba* is the unity of the three; the *aveṣṭhāḥ* is the fourfold terminal enveloping.
"Ascend upwards, excluding the lower half; one should know that it has two windings.
"The brilliance of Soma is twice-wrapped; the two golden-formed ones have three windings.
"Soma, may you be wrapped within; [the brilliance] of the mountain has three windings. (37–38)
"To Prajāpati," [he says] for the double-layered; "O Rudra, that which is thy inner layering," [he says];
"Thee, the inner layering of Indra," [he says]; "Thee, the double-layered for Agni," [he says].
"The Haṃsa for the double-layered verse," [he says]; "That thou art, O pleasant one, and the inner layering," [he says].
The conqueror sat down, overcoming the two-fold nature through the fourfold unity with Ādi (40).
Through Savitṛ he attained the two-fold, through the Aśvins the pair; the three-fold and the two-fold, while uniting, he took up the pair-unity among the seven (41).

The hands and so forth are fourfold; the two-fold and three-fold [verses] proceed in pairs; the unity of the pair follows; the eleven [deities] follow the fire; the two-fold [verses] of the earth have their common abode in the three-fold;
the back of the waters is two-fold; the two-fold [verses] are for the two [worlds]; the three-fold is the encircling of the year. 42.
O Agni, you [are praised] in the fifteen-fold [stoma]; the two-fold and three-fold [stomas are] the bull-like Agni for you (43).
The plants are eleven; from them the two-fold [stoma] arises. Having made the head of Makha, that [sacrifice] should be bound with two [strands]; the Vasus are the inner-binders for you (44).
"Aditi [has bound] you with a single bond; Mitra's bond is twofold. Having stood up, [he recites] "The Great One" and so forth—these two [verses]. "The inner enclosure," 45.
And in all [the verses] beginning with "Do not," there are two-fold [and] three-fold food-offerings, O Lord of Food.

The *dvivṛd* is seen in the *adhyāya*; you are the *dvisuparṇa*, and there is the unity of nine. 46. "You are consciousness" (*cidasīti*) at the end of the increase; there is the *sañjñāna* and the triple encircling.
For the *anuvāka* consists of the *dvivṛt*; "You are firm" (*dhruvāsīti*), and there is the unity of four. 47.

From the verse "kāṇḍāt," there are four [verses] consisting of two-fold repetitions; the Virāj, Jyotis, and Traya-ekatā, as well as the Aṣāḍhā and others, should likewise be nineteen, with two enclosures (dviveṣṭana).
"imammā syā" is three-fold (trivṛt); "ekaśaphaṃ paśum" is two-fold (dvivṛt).
The goat has a thousand woolly fibers, for it is devoid of an end and has two windings.
O youngest one, you are to be doubly wound; "apāntvam" is the final winding.
This new one is not to be wound in front, for it is twice-folded except for the final half. 49–50.
*Dhruvakṣitiḥ* in four [sections], *dvivṛt* in two; with *adityās tvā* there is a triple-envelopment (*triveṣṭana*).
With *sajūr mūrdhā vacaḥ*, etc., up to the end of the section, it is a single-envelopment (*ekaveṣṭana*).
*Indrāgnī* would be a double-envelopment (*dvivṛt*); *viśvakarmā tvā* is a pair in unity (*yugalaikatā*).
The first [section] consists of the *mūrdhan* and the *aśu* hymns of Agni; the *bharga* and *eka* hymns follow according to the sequence of the *anuvākas*. 52.

The *dvivṛt* and *trivṛt* hymns of Agni, the *sahas*, the *purīṣa* of Agni, the *dvivṛt*, and likewise the *ādya*, *raśmin*, *rājñī*, and *ayaṃ puraḥ* hymns follow according to the sequence of the *anuvākas*. 53.
The *agnirmūrdhā* section is a two-fold repetition (*dviveṣṭya*), with three windings (*triveṣṭana*) at its end;
the *yena ṛṣayaḥ* section is a two-fold repetition (*dvivṛt*) with five windings at the end.
In the *prodha* section, excluding the two-fold repetition and the final winding, there are indeed two repetitions and a winding at the end.
Salutations to you! Among the seven sections (anuvākas), the first has two "enclosures" (veṣṭanas).
In the six sections ending with *vṛt*, there are six; in the eight beginning with *drāpe andhas*, there are two enclosures.
In this [section] beginning with *daśāsmin mahati*, all have enclosures at the end. 55–56.
From us this vigor, this expansion, comes; the three are one, the ocean is sevenfold, the expansion—homage to your heat, O expansion! 57.
Those gods among the gods who are double-folded, being invoked, are within the enclosure.
That [section] of Savitṛ consists of five; the *śukrajyotis* section occurs twice (58).
This *dvivṛt* section consists of these *anuvākas*; "etā arṣati" is a *trivṛt*; the *anuvākas* beginning with "vāja" should have their concluding sections bound together (59).
The *anuvāka* beginning with "dvivṛd vājasya" has two verses; "payaḥ pṛthivyām" has one;
"ṛtāṣṭakā" has one; "ekarucā" has one; "udvayoḥ" has two; "parītā" has one at the end.
In the three [sections] beginning with "hy agnim" and in the initial *anuvākas*, there are two verses each.

The word *svādūnnit* (ending in *ū* and having an udātta accent on the first syllable) is repeated twice; *parītī* (ending in *ī*) is repeated twice; *dvirvāyoḥ* (the word *vāyu* preceded by *dviḥ*) is repeated three times;
*punāti te* (the word *te* following *punāti*) is repeated twice. (61) Words ending in *brahma*, *kṣatra*, or *nāman* are repeated twice;

words ending in *garga*, *ardha*, *anta*, or *vṛd* are repeated twice; words ending in *tejas* or *vṛdh* are repeated twice when followed by *āśvinam*; and words such as *vyāghra* are repeated twice when followed by *ādi*. (62)
In the twenty-six mantras, there should be the *svadhā* ending for the ancestors (*pitṛbhyas*).
In twelve [mantras], there is a double repetition; in [the mantra] "O Maruts, eat the oblation" (*marṭha haviḥ*), there is a triple repetition (63).
In the [mantras] beginning with "May they rise up" (*udīratām*), there is a double repetition, but the wrapping belongs only to the sequence.
By you, the first [layer] should be wound around once, and the hair-like [threads] twice;
one should exclude the Śūdra and the Vaiśya from the chapter on the gods, and that [chapter] should have half of all [the layers] wrapped around.
And for the Śūdra, it should be without mantras; in the place of the ancestors, the other [layer] is twice.

In the *imam me varuna* and other [sections], the goat (*chāga*) occurs at the end of the second *trivṛt*; in the *yakṣat* sections, it occurs at the end of the third *trivṛt*. Following that, the two *aśvin* sections have the goat at the beginning; thereafter, the two *aśvin* sections have the goat at the end, followed by the *vanaspati* and *agni* sections, which conclude with the goat.

In the *devabarhi* and other [mantras], there is a doubling of the deity, for the deity is indeed completely enveloped (67). In the [mantras] "agnim adya" and "sūpasthā tvām adya," there is a triad becoming one; because of the increase of light at the end, there is the designation of "doubling," while there is a unification of the pair (68).
The two *vṛdhi*s for Agni, the *vṛt* of the *anuvāka* beginning with *hiraṇyapāṇi*, and the *dviveṣṭana* of the *vājījana*;
the *kāya* and others of the *anuvāka*, and indeed the *antaveṣṭana*. 69.
In the chapter beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha," there is the Prajāpati [verse] ending in "antaḥ" (70).
"Yaḥ prāṇataḥ" is a two-versed [section]; "candramāḥ" is its extreme enclosure. In the three [verses] beginning with "yujanti," there are the Vasus; it is the unity of the pair (71).
Is it in four? Or would there be Vāyu in five, with a double wrapping? Agni is the animal, excluding the middle; here, the unity of the two is doubled.
(72) In the five Anuvākas beginning with *utsakthya*, there would be a double wrapping.
Beginning with the horse, there is unity up to the end of the *soma* and other offerings (73).
From the *rohit* onwards, joined by two [others], there is unity from the *śitirandhra* with its inner wrapping, the *śuddhavāla*, and so on, up to the end of the *avadruti* (74).

The *vṛddhiyukta*, *phalagvāmi*, *dvaikya*, and *śilpa* [are the names of sections]; likewise, the *antavṛt* occurs within the seven *anuvākas*. In these [sections], there is the *antaveṣṭana* (encircling) of the mantras.
Furthermore, the *śāda* occurs in the nine *anuvākas*, and the *anuvākavṛt* [occurs] in the ninth *anuvāka*.
In the five *mūrdhan* sections, one should know the *dvivṛt* and the *anuvāka* as *dvivṛt* (76);
"Agniśca" is *trivṛt*, and in the three intervening [sections] there is *dvivṛt*; indeed, one should know the *vaiśvānara* as *trivṛt* and "Agnir ukthena" as *antavṛt* (77).

In the *vaiśvānara* section, there are six [sections] beginning with *mumatā*, having two enclosures (*dviveṣṭana*), and the chapter ending with *dvivṛtsamāstvā* has one enclosure (*adhyāya-cid-antya-veṣṭana*). 78.
The section beginning with *saṃvatsaro 'si dvivṛt* is the *anuvākavṛt*.
The Hotṛ should sacrifice with the eleven [verses] beginning with "pūrvaścaiva," and the next is the two-fold (dvivṛt) [verse]. 79.
The next is Devabarhis, the two-fold [verse], Śuci, Uṣṇih, Mātrikā, and Ūrdhvā; among these, at the ends of the half-gaṇas, there are those respective mantras ending in "śata" and "vṛt. 80.
In the two [sections] at the end, beginning with "dviveṣṭam indrāya vayodhase," all the mantras in the section starting from "samiddho añjan" are *dviveṣṭana*.
For the three final *anuvākas*, the procedure is that of an *anuvāka*.
The two chapters beginning with "dvivṛd" and "asyājarā," as well as the one ending with "bṛhan nid," [are included].

(82) The chapter beginning with "dvivṛd yajjāgrataḥ," the one ending with "dyubhir aktubhiḥ," and the one containing "viśvāni ca vibhaktāram"; however, the others are merely enclosures (*veṣṭanāḥ*). (83)
In the *Sahasraśīrṣā* hymn among the twenty-four [hymns], this [Purusha] is twice-fold, not thrice-fold; he is like the sky among the ten [directions], twice-fold.
With the days of the threefold [sacrifice], the twice-fold Vāyu purifies.
Savitṛ is threefold, another is threefold, the earth is two-fold, and the sky is two-fold (85).

The *ṛc* is threefold, the *vacas* is threefold, that which is within me is two-fold, and the one who encircles is accompanied by aids; in the four beginning with "kayā tvam" (RV 4.31.1), it is two-fold (86).

"Day and night, the threefold goddess, for our well-being"—thus [is the mantra]. The heaven is the double-layered peace; there should be inner wrappings. Without [it], it is firm indeed; the triple-wrapping is for long life.
Homage to you, the inner-wrapping; from that, let the eye be the double-layered.
"Ādade devi devyaśca," "iti indraikyaṃ praitu," and "makhasya aśvasya" each consist of nine verses; "yamāya" consists of three verses;
the *anuvāka* beginning with "dvivṛdgarbhaḥ" consists of three verses, excluding the final verse of the "viśvāsa" section. 88–89.

One who takes up each group of four—namely *yaste*, *dvivṛt*, *paraḥ*, and *antavṛt*—that constitutes one for *samudrāya*; that which consists of two, three, and one (*dvitryaikyam*) is for *yamāya* with two enclosures (90);
*viśvā āśāḥ* is the sum of five groups of one; *svāhā pūṣṇe* follows the pattern of the Anuvāka.
The *abhimantṛ* [section] is divided into two; the fourfold unity is in the Ṛc, and the twofold division extends as far as the end of the *yāvatī* Anuvāka.
Then follows the *iṣas* up to the end of the *saṃvṛk*; the eight *svāhā-prāṇa* Anuvākas are like the [preceding] Anuvākas. 91–92.
For length, there is the singleness of the *yuga*; for *Yama*, there is the final wrapping (93). "This whole world is enveloped by the Lord"—this is to be wrapped twice, as agreed upon by all (94).
Thus ends the *Kramakārikā-śikṣā*.
